featured.title: Security Begins with Breach
featured.subtitle: Joe Nehila on LinkedIn

slides.title: Security Begins with Breach
slides.subtitle: Joe Nehila on LinkedIn
slides.description: A friend of mine starts every security engagement with a PowerPoint where he presents compelling statistics (costs and personnel requirements) associated with breaching security (physical or cyber). For the past few months, I have included this statement in my cover letters when applying for security and cybersecurity roles: ... many large, reputable firms do not take an “assumed breach” approach to their security planning. I do not know what kind of environment ABC CORP is; if my cover letter does nothing for my candidacy but finds your eyes, I want to tell you ... that you are almost definitely breached. This is how I end the letter: Approaching planning from [an assumed breach] perspective allows an organization to not just be “reactive,” but “proactive” with their security posture as they improve processes and solve scaled problems. My colleague tells me if the firm is not willing to adopt an assumed breach philosophy, he refuses to provide a long-term engagement. Not every firm has been breached, but if you are large enough to have a security team (or if you are small but in a meaningful space: space, autonomous vehicles, telecom, etc), you are a target and considering who the threat actors are that would be interested in your IP, data, etc. is vital. At a certain size or based on the info you possess, you are definitely breached - or could be quickly by a determined adversary (creating a Schrödinger's cyber-cat scenario). Assumed breach is often a mantra that only a single group or person will live by in a company, almost a voice crying in the wilderness that others view as being "pessimistic" or "doomsday." Coworkers can feel as if they are being second-guessing and the corporation's accomplishments or capabilities are underrepresented because a colleague assumes breach. Maybe there is a misapprehension that taking an assumed breach stance is akin to waving a white flag, saying that the enemy is within our system, so why even try. This could not be further from the truth. I count myself as highly optimistic. My friend is one of the most kind-hearted, jovial individuals you will ever meet. No one who knows my colleague would describe him as negative; heck, he might even be TOO nice! Rather than discounting your org, their accomplishments, the quality of their personnel, or declaring defeat, assuming breach informs your framework and planning from a much maligned yet incredibly important start point that will save you time, money, and if your firm is significant, embarrassment. That is why to insist on an assumed breach posture. Tell me what you think about my take on the problem, suggestion for assumed breach approach and conclusion. The Problem Exigency When is the right time to start applying an assumed breach approach to security (especially cybersecurity) planning? Why do it at all? How crucial is it? First, let us all agree on a common set of arguments. What is publicly disclosed about attacks and breaches is the "tip of the iceberg." We can infer a limited range of capabilities and interests based on available data. We can apply known motivations to establish adversary objectives. First-hand and reliable second-hand experience can sharpen our analysis. Therefore, we should all agree that our analysis of the depth and gravity of cybersecurity threats is substantially limited by our available data. Our available data is a limited dataset and our experiences as well as indicators from our adversaries allow us to create a more reliable bounding of their plans, intentions and capabilities (PIC). Disclosures So how vast is the threat landscape and how deeply do we need to worry? Let's look from a standpoint of United States public and private interests, e.g. keeping people safe, safeguarding privacy, personally identifiable information (PII), and intellectual property. It would be reasonable to turn a mirror and reflect it upon non-US interest actors as well (with US interest actor being defined as our government, military, institutions, businesses, systems, public servants, and private citizens without regard to legal status as long as they support Democracy, civil liberties and a "free market" as championed by the United States). With all our caveating out of the way, the threats are wide ranging, both a mile wide and a mile deep, asymmetric and motley! It's hard to decide if the best way to demonstrate the severity of this issue is to present examples based on threat actor or how serious a breach is; for my part, I've decided to go for severity and complexity of target as a measurement to demonstrate why Breach is the only place to start security planning. What's the Worst Thing You Can Imagine? If you were going to think about some of the most critical information in our country and those systems, you'd be hard pressed to overlook the people that work for the United States Government, its cyber A-Team and Linux. The OPM Breach If ever you were going to protect something, it would be who has security clearances and all the SF-86 forms which contain crazy detailed and very intimate info about personal life, family members, finances, and contacts. In 2015, reportedly the Chinese Government accessed a treasure trove of information about current, former, and prospective US Government employees as well as many visitors to USG Facilities. At the House committee meeting, OPM Chief Information Officer Donna Seymour disclosed not only the SF-86 but comprehensive adjudication information (all the processing nitty gritty) was breached. There are separate systems in place for certain government agencies and it was not disclosed if such systems have information crossover or if PII from those systems was breached (such conversation would likely have taken place under the auspices of a classified addendum). "NSA" Tools in the Wild Rank ordering sensitive digital materials, you'd have to put tools developed by the National Security Agency (NSA), the US Government's premier cyber and crypto organization, top of the list. As most readers will remember, in 2017 the "Shadow Brokers" (SB) disclosed they came into possession of tools from Equation Group (EG, an APT ascribed to the NSA); SB gave some tools away to promote auctioning the others off. More recently, some have linked the same group to Tweets not just in 2017, but in August of 2016 and a question arose based on the use of some of the exploits as early as March on targets incompatible with EG interests and believed to be connected to Buckeye (APT 3 associated with China). Analysts, at least publicly, remain unsure of SB's origin and considered Russia the leading contender in public discourse. Suddenly, the earlier sightings complicate matters, indicating Buckeye got the same tools earlier, reverse engineered EG tools, SB got the tools from Buckeye, or EG themselves to name a few scenarios. Whatever happened, these tools in the wild gave birth to some of the most insidious ransomware attacks, including WannaCry and NotPetya and proved one or more APTs were susceptible to breach. (Lest Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) folks say, "at least our tools were not leaked," there was obviously THIS which hinged on an insider threat.) Decade of the Rats Just when everyone thinks Blackberry is totally out of the game, they publish a scintillating report in 2020. I borrow their wording: "Groups associated with the state or state-sponsored efforts of at least three governments have been found to develop and deploy Linux malware: China, Russia, and the United States. A class of Linux malware called Derusbi has been known to be used by APT groups acting in the interest China, including LEVIATHAN (APT40), DEEP PANDA, AXIOM, and APT41 (MITRE, 2017). In 2014, Kaspersky discovered that the Russian group TURLA was also deploying Linux malware (Baumgartner & Raiu, 2014), and another group Kaspersky identifies as THE EQUATION GROUP (generally thought to be the NSA) has also targeted Linux servers extensively." Of course, three years earlier the FBI quietly indicted a former IBM worker and "Linux kernel hacker" on charges of economic espionage, which may have reached back to 2014 (the same time as an extensive Chinese Linux botnet operation was underway). The kernel-level rootkits discussed by Blackberry have significant implications and suggest a much wider compromise of Linux systems throughout the 2010s, a system which is the backbone of pretty much everything. (NB. This same Blackberry report talks about Android exploitation...) So, in the last decade, an APT comprehensively compromised all the onboarding and clearance information for at least a large portion of USG employees, cyber tools believed to be connected to the NSA, and Linux. These major breaches prove all actors and all data is vulnerable to breach. [For an awesome and extensive list of breaches, check out this work done by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) (2006-Present) and Tavish Vaidya from Georgetown University (2001-2013).] Determined Adversaries These three major breaches also demonstrate determined adversaries can get access to just about (let's hedge just a little) any system on the planet. Security incidents are not limited to Information Technology (IT) systems, but Operational Technology (OT) systems are compromised as well. Namely, OT has emerged in the state vs. state race with Stuxnet, Estonia, Georgia, Ukraine, Israel, Iran and the United States power grid having all been in the news. In this space, small scale attacks and issues should not be dismissed as they may be dry runs in testing capabilities. Russia has been aggressive in its use of cyber strikes while prosecuting armed conflicts throughout Eastern Europe and will likely continue to use this as a primary means of reducing the loss of Russian human life during conflicts, especially considering the lack of notable international repercussion. Cyber is a high stakes game of financial investment, allocating resources, tool development, reputational risk, and never knowing when you have crossed a red line. Specifically, cyber, when it crosses over into OT, can cause significant risk to human life. Whether the threat actor who attacked Israel's water system planned to get people sick (as the Chlorine level change would not have been enough to kill people according to reporting), get people within a limited geography sick (maybe where a military base is), see if it worked (test of capability) or miscalculated somehow, it is not clear. (As a side note, it would not be fair to specifically blame Iran; Iran may have deployed the threat or they may have been complicit by allowing a proxy, such as Hezbollah. Even further, they may have been permitting a threat actor to operate within their border, they could have provided training, vulnerabilities or digital resources [VPNs/servers] and therefore been the subject of retaliation for aiding and abetting the attackers.) It can also not be overstated that early state-level cyberattacks have tested the strength of international treaties and the results have not been promising to global blue teams. The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) did not respond when Russia used cyber warfare on Estonia, Georgia and later Ukraine, under multiple administrations. In each case Russia proceeded with little geopolitical ramification to both their cyberattacks and eventual border incursions. Adversaries have also accessed user information for popular gaming platforms like Sony and Nintendo, they've hit credit reporting firms, banking institutions, and the list goes on and on. I was particularly impressed by one enterprising team of cyber criminals who managed to trick an employee of Norway's state investment fund to transfer them $10mm through an email scam. This would also be a suitable area to mention breach is not just related to a cyberattack and digital persistence. Breaches can be human-enabled (witting and unwitting), extensive technical operations, supply chain operations, hinge on paid insiders, be a run-of-the-mill insider threat posed by a dissatisfied employee, and much more. Any disclosures that compromise the safety of employees, customers, clients, and IP matters, whether it was a highly sophisticated zero day enabling a state-of-the-art tool, an over-the-counter use of MetaSploit, or a would-be Robin Hood that turns out less the "devilishly delightful rogue" and more like a bridge troll. So you are defending against incredibly determined adversaries - capable individuals, a thousand grains of sand, hired guns, organized crime, state sanctioned thieves, the economically down-and-out willing to compromise their integrity - and unfortunately, even internal witting or unwitting accomplices to ne'er-do-wells. Why Cyberattack? Most organizations use a cost-benefit analysis when considering how they will operate. Non-state and state actor decision calculus varies. Organized cyber criminals have little compunction when it comes to who they hurt, most often feeling their crimes are victimless thanks to insurance, banking institutions, and their imaginations about the bottomless pockets of businesses (especially those in "wealthy" countries). With the rule of law being moderate at best in many locations where these individuals thrive, namely Southeast Asia, Eastern Europe and Africa, the cost is low and the benefit potential is jets and Ferraris... let alone some operate in jurisdictions where the government takes a blatant blind-eye approach. We have also made access to cyber tools easy, not just with EQ's tool breach, but in general with the willingness to create cyber pyramid schemes with OG bad guys creating ransomware tools and licensing them for a cut to script kiddies all over the world. Wireshark and Metasploit are easy to run and torrents abound. This means the barrier for entry is quite low with the payoffs extremely high. One criminal ring, GandCrab, self-reportedly generated $2 billion USD during their time running a ransomware "profit share" "Ransom as a Service" (RaaS) enterprise. The barrier for entry, even on the technical front, is essentially null. Notably, part of the GandCrab user agreement was not targeting CIS countries (Commonwealth of Independent States aka the former Soviet Block minus Poland and EU-leaning Eastern European countries). This takes us to the next reason to commit cyber crimes, you have some state actors who are complicit either in using the "business" to bolster their own coffers (read: North Korea), who are easily bought off or who just don't care. The above link regarding the would-be hacking journalist notes his lawyer mentioning "...if I got the impression I was about to do business with the North Korean government or some other sanctioned entity, I should get back in touch with him." There are many state sponsors to cyber theft with the Sony hack being one of the largest on record. The notable millennial cybercriminal, Evil Corp's aqua, has a $5 million reward, yet is safeguarded inside Russia because his crimes largely benefit their elite and focus on Western interests. In some instances it is difficult to identify who the cyber-perpetrators are, and in other instances, the host government allows them to operate with impunity. There is also the uncomfortable question of how these funds might be used to mount covert paramilitary campaigns around the world at a state level. Not all cyber criminals live in their grandmother's basements or operate to get themselves and oligarch backers even richer. Nor, for that matter, can we assume that all of criminals are in it strictly for a better paying job (the average per capita income in Belarus was $4,122 in 2019 and $785 in the Democratic Republic of Congo; it's easy to see how obtaining a few thousand USD for bringing down a small healthcare provider with ransomware would be an attractive enterprise). If the Iran-Contra affair taught the world anything, it is that governments find unusual vehicles to quietly finance their proxy wars. And that's if you're not a heavily sanctioned state that just plain needs the money (North Korea). It is my honest assessment that the United States Government learned from the ICA and do not condone such enterprises but I believe the US is in the minority, or a narrow majority at best. Ultimately, cyber attacks are lower risk and come with minimal international blowback. This makes them an ideal vehicle for enterprising, unscrupulous and/or desperate criminals to make a living, especially in a low to moderate rule-of-law country. Beyond this, they are a great way of obtaining PII for governments who want to thwart foreign adversaries as well as internal opposition. Cyber is necessary to combat international terrorism. Often, dissidents are targeted by regimes looking to maintain authority and cultural organizations judged to pose a potential threat to hegemonic order are also routinely targeted. Thus far, the geopolitical, state-level, proportionate response to cyber attacks has also been low-key, from a similar attack performed against an adversary's equities to kicking out a few diplomats in protest. I'd be remiss to not consider Israel's airstrike against Hamas in 2019, but this was a first-of-its-kind act and against a non-sovereign entity with which there has been a long-standing armed conflict. This strike smacked of a "don't make me do it" style retaliation to set a clear boundary with Hamas regarding Israel's tolerance for cyberwarfare. By contrast, Russia has, without compunction, used cyber and acted with aggression throughout Eastern Europe and not been the target of reprisals by NATO or other international organizations. China has also prosecuted intrusive and extensive campaigns against Taiwan, Hong Kong, the United Kingdom and United States. Iran and North Korea have crossed red lines using cyber and not seen any military action as a result. One should not dismiss the culpability of the United States and their other "Five Eyes" partners (Canada, United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand) in the global cyber scene. Citizens can be grateful that our government's actions have not limited our abilities to travel internationally or threatened the peace and security we generally feel living in the US and abroad. They've resulted in diplomats having a bad day and a non-stop cyber-wave threatening our most sensitive everything. This is what makes cyber so attractive and, when coupled with cost considerations, communicates private industry needs to fully adapt a "breach philosophy" for productive blue team work. (For a digression, try this article, "Can a Cyberattack Ever Rise to an "Act of War.") Global Cyber Threats and Private Industry In 2019, 20 exploited zero days were found in the wild through Project Zero Day. It would be reasonable to assume that at least as many were quietly patched without disclosures, and as many exist that have yet to be discovered. This would mean, if one made some reasonable logical leaps, 80 zero days were used/active globally in 2019. Many security teams have bug bounties and benefit from white hat hackers/researchers willing to supply vulnerability data. Grey Hats are often happy to sell their exploits to the highest bidder. You do not generally read after-action reports of patched CVEs; the results of a patch that does not actually "kick" someone from a network enjoy little interest outside industry insiders. This all assumes the need for a unique exploit rather than adversaries exploiting old systems and lax patching. The most common vectors for breach are unupdated software/systems, poorly configured systems/password issues, and insiders. What then should we assume is the global breadth of threat if zero day exploits could only reasonably be considered a small percentage of breaches? The stage has been set for the severity of the issue, the opportunity for attack, the willingness of threat actors to take action, and the ramifications of actions taken on a global scale. The final element is tying these threats into the private landscape. It would be trivial to just cut and paste dozens of attacks to say, "it's been done before." I believe this does not work because those in cybersecurity often feel a sense of bias towards their own solutions and adequacy of addressing challenges. Who would ever go to their boss and say "we are in trouble"?!?!! Who wants to walk up to their CEO and say," whatever we do will never be enough, but we should try anyway, and we should spend more money trying!" That's crazy talk! I understand. And yet, that is the reality. A determined adversary will pierce your corporate defenses. Northrop Grumman came under "cyberattack" in 2011 as did Lockheed Martin and L-3. If 2011 was not bad enough, more weapons information was stolen in 2013. Yahoo made news for a massive hack in 2014 that supposedly compromised 500 million accounts; then the news hit that a year earlier they'd been breached, 500 million turned into 1 billion. Following Yahoo's acquisition by Verizon, Verizon announced in 2017 that the hack had actually compromised every single Yahoo account at that time. This hack turned out to be a Russian security service operation to surreptitiously access designated email accounts. At first Yahoo approached the FBI believing some 26 accounts had been compromised; later the forensic examiners confirmed over 6,400 emails were accessed by Russian agents. Whether one wants to blame a cover-up mentality trying to protect shareholders, national security, credit a new set of eyes, the improvements in digital forensics over that time period or our evolution in understanding tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs), one cannot help but observe the delays in disclosure and the very big difference between 500 million and 3 billion! Finally, who can forget the Equifax hack where, based on the common vulnerability and exposure (CVE) identified, Chinese hackers were in the system for at least 134 days (this must be read as a minimum given pivoting) and managed to acquire PII for 147.9 million Americans. Around the same time, Deloitte reported at hack that turned out to last at least from Oct 2016 - Sep 2017. Truly there is a dead cyber-cat in our black boxes. Fin These should be illustrative examples for several reasons. The primary three takeaways are, first, secrets being held by a large, well funded defense contractor were not safe once or even twice (is it worth pointing out the same defense contractors are hired on contracts to provide cybersecurity to the USG?). Second, our initial assessment of the gravity of cyberattacks could reasonably be characterized as often incorrect. Finally, third, persistences (cyberattacks that lead to access to a system) often begin far earlier than we realize. In sum, there is no panacea that suddenly provides immunization for cyber, no matter how sensitive our data, breaches are often far worse than we realize and have been going on for far longer than we assess. OUCH! Who can blame co-workers and management for being a little defensive when a well-meaning cybersecurity analyst or engineer suggests a "breach" approach, trying to communicate the inherent and far-reaching risks posed by APTs, cyber criminals and threat actors. After all, many enterprises are trying to turn their cybersecurity cost centers into profitable "as a service" units or creators of valuable IP. There has been a long-standing tug-and-pull related to showing "value" in cybersecurity. Why then would it be exciting to insinuate that the service or product provider may already be the victim of a breach and not even know it? Well, we care about foreign governments targeting dissidents, terrorists using our systems to murder innocent people, and potential abuses of our technology. We also care about having functioning backups lest we become a victim like Garmin in a nasty ransomware attack. However, we are also equally concerned about divorcees whose are manipulated by "romance" scammers and small businesses ripped off by bogus money-transfer requests. These scams are enabled by stolen databases of public and private records, scraping, and passing information through the dark web. Victims and many others have their PII stolen, deal with years of nasty personality theft issues and are routinely financially wounded. It is equally embarrassing to that finagled parent who sent their "Canadian-lover" money for a plane ticket as it is to that Norwegian banker. We care because we care about people first and it informs the actions we know we need to take. None of what I have shared should be a source of embarrassment for any of these organizations; we need to expect that breaches do and will occur and plan accordingly. This is what a presumed breach philosophy is. Threat actors may arise as a single smart person, a small team, RaaS, or be a well-funded group working for the government; they may also bootstrap their own business enterprise as cybercriminals. The wide range of threats, adversaries and motivations lead to blue teams always feeling like they are on an arduous security hike uphill, in the snow, in a storm, barefoot. In a nutshell, this is why security begins with breach; as it happens, we have two choices, we can wait until we find a breach to start reacting to breach or we can act as if there is a breach and try to root out vulnerabilities, threat actors, and protect our most valuable data by design, from the beginning.

publications.title: Merging physical and digital engineering can help transportation agencies work smarter and faster
publications.description:
Many forward-looking departments of transportation across the United States are beginning to look and work very differently than they did a decade ago. Some are rolling out generative AI pilots to flag pedestrian safety risks. Others are rebuilding their business systems to unify planning, budgeting, and project delivery. In places like Broward County, Florida, transportation planners are using digital twins to make better planning decisions.1

These aren’t just upgrades; they mark a deeper shift, from physical-first operations to a digitally fueled system-of-systems digital infrastructure backbone, where data, digital tools (such as AI, 3D models, and digital twins), and real-time intelligence work in sync to address key transportation problems. The goal is richer situational and operational awareness, with the help of systems that can sense what’s happening across the network, share that insight across departments and jurisdictions, and guide faster, smarter decisions.

Why now? Because the traditional model (building bridges, resurfacing highways, maintaining critical infrastructure) isn’t keeping up. Demands on infrastructure routinely exceed DOT resources across all categories. Costs are rising, delivery is getting more challenging, staff capacity continues to shrink, and the issues DOTs face—from rising congestion and road safety to uneven growth and regional planning—are substantially more complex and interconnected. Fortunately, DOTs have a wealth of data that can be leveraged through digital engineering to unlock deeper insights and more efficient and targeted solutions.

The physical infrastructure backbone remains critically important, but it is no longer sufficient. DOTs need a new way of working that connects core engineering with digital intelligence across the infrastructure lifecycle... 

We explore how DOTs across the United States are beginning to make that shift and what it will take for others to follow.

publications.title: Dynamic AI Governance: A Recipe for Crafting Trustworthy AI
publications.description: For government leaders tasked with implementing responsible and effective AI solutions, prioritizing a cohesive AI governance strategy that works with its people’s existing tendencies for governance is likely critical to success. Currently, three personas represent the three common approaches to effective AI governance: Guides, who focus on enterprise policymaking like Executive Order 14110; Guards, who focus on standardized quality assurance checkpoints; and Gadgeteers, who focus on tooling and feedback mechanisms. While these approaches can provide a strong foundation, the exponential pace of AI innovation should have dynamic AI governance that can integrate all three approaches and adapt as AI continues to evolve.

publications.title: The Evolving Tolling Landscape: Improving Toll Revenue Collection in Electronic Tolling
publications.description:
The techniques used to levy tolls on roads, bridges, and tunnels have changed dramatically in the last 30 years. With new technologies that permit traffic to flow freely as toll authorities collect payments digitally, current roadways should be at peak efficiency. Yet current estimates indicate that US toll authorities are unable to collect at least $2.24 billion annually due to various breakdowns in the
collection process.

publications.title: Digital Engineering and Digital Twin in the Space Industry
publications.description: The space industry is rapidly accelerating toward a trillion-dollar valuation. As the sector is ramping up with an increased number of space launches, missions, and innovative breakthroughs, efficient digital engineering can ease cost and resource burdens. In addition, the use of digital twins—virtual representations of assets—can reduce risk around launch logistics and awareness of objects in space. Deloitte's capabilities can help public sector space agencies take a problem-centric approach to digital twinning opportunities.

publications.title: Metaverse
publications.description:
Gather in the same room with friends spread across the globe, have a conversation with Albert Einstein, feel what it is like to fly like a bird. The metaverse is bringing ideas from science fiction into today's reality. While many of the metaverse headlines are in media and entertainment – such as Meta's $10B investment – the public sector is also already well down the path towards the metaverse with the Bahamas rolling out a nationwide metaverse in education and the US Army investing up to $22B on augmented reality systems for soldiers as just two examples. The impact of these systems on public sector operations is likely to be significant. The metaverse can make maintenance more efficient, cities smarter and improve readiness of government workforce through simulated trainings. This report will introduce you to these and many more applications of the metaverse for government.
With new opportunities come new challenges
But new technologies also introduce new challenges that the public sector will need help navigating. Not only is it difficult to choose the right technology to solve a problem, but also to get the best out of the metaverse, many organizations will need to modernize underlying technology. Perhaps more pressing is the need to understand how the metaverse may introduce needs for new regulation or new forms of infrastructure. After all, it has been only a little over ten years since most Americans began using broadband internet, and broadband connectivity is today nearly as important as water or electricity infrastructure. Public sector clients will need help navigating both these opportunities and these challenges, and this document can help give you a head start on those conversations.

publications.title: NFTs
publications.description: Built on a blockchain foundation, non-fungible tokens, or NFTs, are a sizable and growing market. While NFTs have gained traction in the commercial market, GPS market adoption is still nascent though expected to grow comparable to the blockchain market. Current blockchain pilots are not yet able to scale. Clients will likely face 4 barriers when exploring the use of NFTs–many of which are tied to challenges of the underlying blockchain tech.

publications.title: Tolling Revenue Leakage
publications.description: The shift from cash based tolling to electronic tolling collection (ETC)* has resulted in US tolling authorities missing out on an estimated $2.24 billion per year in uncollected revenue due to challenges throughout the toll by plate process. Along some toll corridors, nearly 50% of drivers not using a transponder (e.g., E ZPass ) use the roads for free despite willingness to pay. Most tolling revenue leakage occurs during the invoicing process due inaccurate information capture from the vehicle’s license plate, unreliable or inaccessible address information, and/or inconsistent or unclear payment options for customers

publications.title: Data Trust & Integrity
publications.description: Government agencies and corporations use increasingly large amounts of data to make and defend a host of decisions. With the increase in data comes an increased chance of malicious data manipulation. A market gap exists around tools to ascertain whether data being used to drive decision making has been manipulated at some point and how much the data can be trusted in the present stage of its lifecycle. Many data threats exist today, including two primary threat types: Disinformation false content that is deliberately spread and intended to mislead in order to influence or obscure the truth (e.g., deep fakes) and Data Hiding content that is modified by hiding information within the original data or metadata (e.g., steganography)

publications.title: Beyond Buzz Words: What the Data Says About PM Skills for Digital Business
publications.description:
Project management office (PMO) leaders observe a growing misalignment between their project managers’ skill sets and today’s rapidly changing solutions delivery landscape. As a result, more than two thirds of PMO leaders report that updating their project management competency models is a high priority for the near term.

Our skills model can help PMO leaders rapidly upskill their staff to prepare for digital business. Newly revised for digital business, this competency model draws upon analysis of a survey of more than 8,600 project managers at more than 240 large enterprises.

publications.title: Evolving for Digital Business: 6 Key Roles for Today's PMO
publications.description: Digital business is forcing PMO leaders to reevaluate the function’s mandate. Depending on the context and existing capabilities, leading PMOs support the enterprise by playing a combination of six key roles critical to digital business transformation: investment steward, orchestrator, promoter, talent enabler, program driver and service provider.

publications.title: Standing up with Standing Teams
publications.description: In 2018, almost half of companies are organizing their delivery staff in standing teams, i.e., a resourcing model of permanent teams, which contain nearly all staff required for end-to-end project execution. This general shift in the way teams are staffed will impact the project manager role in three ways: (1) project management touchpoints on project-by-project execution will decline, (2) project management will look increasingly like program management, and (3) project managers will offer two-in-a-box support to product owners.

publications.title: Core Attributes of Product Line Management
publications.description: The move from projects to products is a central component of The New IT Operating Model for Digital. In the product line model, companies allocate funding and resources to product lines that support their most critical business capabilities. Benefits of product line management include....

publications.title: The Case for Killing the Business Case
publications.description: Organizations typically allocate capital after a steering committee carefully considers the business cases for a long line of competing project proposals. But while today’s business context is radically different than that of just five years ago, the format of the business case at most organizations hasn’t changed much. Organizations are now beginning to achieve scale with iterative and continuous delivery techniques, and are moving to funding larger units of investment (e.g., product lines, value streams, programs). Given this context, business and PMO leaders have begun to question the utility of the traditional, project-level business case creation and review process. Here are the four most important reasons why....

publications.title: The Demise of the PMO? Rebooting Your PMO for Product Lines
publications.description: By the close of 2017, more than half of large enterprises will be in a product line model. For the PMO, the implications of this move are considerable. The project management office’s (PMO’s) direct involvement in project-level execution, reporting, and governance declines as staff and responsibilities reorganize around product lines. As a result, many IT executives question where the PMO fits, if at all. In response, leading organizations are rebooting the PMO’s mandate to help the enterprise meet digital challenges.

publications.title: The PMO's Role in Product Line Management
publications.description: Digitization has penetrated all industries. In response, organizations are reconfiguring their operating models to get faster, become customer-centric, and enable cross-enterprise collaboration. At more than half of organizations, product line management is the most common form of the new operating model. Product line management deeply challenges the traditional value proposition of the project management office (PMO). In the coming years, the PMO’s direct role in project-level execution, reporting, and governance will decline. Leading PMOs have already begun adapting to the changed operating context by playing one or more of the following emerging roles within the organization: product line Promoter, Investment Steward, Orchestrator, Talent Enabler, Service Provider, and Program Driver. PMOs must adapt or see their organizational relevance diminished. The following showcases practical solutions to help PMOs play these new, product-line supporting roles in the organization.

publications.title: When Was the Last Time You Checked Your Project’s Assumptions?
publications.description: The average project business case contains a number of assumptions about external (e.g., input prices) and internal factors (e.g., the availability of critical staff). Despite the importance of these assumptions, relatively few organizations rigorously document them, and still fewer review them at regular intervals to see if they hold true. Based on their past project experience and their proximity to project sponsors, PMs can help ensure the quality of project assumptions in two critical ways.

publications.title: Managing the Risks of 'Too Big to Fail' via Cloud Computing
publications.publishedAt: Global Association of Risk Professionals - Risk Professional · Jun 1, 2012
publications.description:
In general, opportunities to create wealth, and the associated risks that can destroy it, are a result of the financial innovation process that is characteristic of a free and a truly competitive market. This historically self-sustaining process will inevitably continue as long as there are financial products and global markets. However, in an unfettered market, as observed recently, innovation sometimes may conflict with the public good, particularly when it becomes so unbridled that it poses a threat to the stability of global financial markets. Thus, a new balancing act is needed to allow markets to function efficiently and to enable participants to play by the rules of the road.

One way of striking such a balance between innovations and stability is by promoting standardization, transparency and availability of financial data. Advanced cloud analytics - which can rapidly and accurately detect high concentrations of tail risk in the G-SIFIs, their major counterparties and highly leveraged firms -- can help us meet those objectives.

When applied appropriately, through the effective use of tools that analyze and monitor systemic risk to reduce market uncertainty, technological innovations (like cloud computing) can indeed support legislative efforts to temper the excesses of financial innovations. More importantly, these tools can provide risk analysts, policymakers and regulators the context they need to build a risk-based framework to quantify the implicit risks and benefits of the "too big to fail" institutions -- and to make fact-based decisions about whether a G-SIFI should be allowed to fail. Not long ago, assessing the systemic risks of the G-SIFIs was considered a nearly impossible task, but cloud computing has changed the game.

With more than 30 years of leadership, transformation, organizational change management, and strategy experience, Brad is focused on helping utilities and individuals navigate large-scale transformations. 

Brad's experience is centered around helping to address large transformation and talent challenges across a number of situations including: business transformations, technology modernizations, mergers & acquisitions, cyber security, workforce planning and disruptions, and regulatory changes (including NERC, grid modernization, etc.)  He delivers practical and impactful perspectives routed in an understanding of the business, cultural, and regulatory environment of utilities.

Brad holds a MBA from the University of New Brunswick (Canada) and an undergraduate degree in Biochemistry from the University of Ottawa (Canada).  Brad is a 2014 Fellow of Leadership Greater Chicago and a former Canadian Naval Reserve Officer.

headline: Employee Experience & Talent Management
about:
I thrive working in a high performing team, which helps the business deliver an employee experience that resonates with the aspirations of a modern workforce. 

I have helped design, deliver and embed an array of initiatives across the end-to-end employee experience e.g. flex, wellbeing, onboarding, digital systems. During this process I have worked with a range of stakeholders, which includes experience designers, UI designers, change specialists, senior executive team, clinical psychologists, culture consultants, executive coaches and technology implementation teams. 

My consulting experience has taught me various disciplines that help me to conceive, implement and embed talent initiatives. I have worked across different geographies in multicultural environments that helps me be culturally aware and empathetic towards my stakeholders while driving towards meaningful outcomes.

experience.description:
I manage a number of Deloitte NZ’s talent initiatives aimed at improving the end-to-employee experience, which includes DXFlex (flexible working), Wellbeing, Coaching, Puāwai Time (a way to record and reward time spent improve people's employee experience), Welcome to Deloitte (a digital uniquely kiwi onboarding experience) & DXConnect (ServiceNow driven digital front door for our people’s needs)

I work with senior partners of the firm to drive all facets of the employee experience for my business unit from onboarding, performance experience, engagement, and wellbeing. I also have experience in managing employment relation matters that are quite unique to an agile and relentless environment where people are being constantly challenged to solve abstract problems. 

Change is a constant due to new acquisitions, internal merger and a disruptive market. This poses excellent challenges to refine/redefine our talent strategies and customise the way we implement them across different parts of our business having their own sub-cultures and leadership styles. 

My consulting experience constantly drives me to find newer and better ways especially on the talent management front.

Kaushik moved from Deloitte US firm's office in India to Deloitte New Zealand, In this role, Kaushik focused on the people side of change for organisation transformation projects. In any organisation transformation, the way we help people deal with change, define how successfully we are able to achieve our larger project goals.

This means taking a holistic “human capital” view of change that integrates stakeholder engagement, communications, training, and a robust post implemenation support network.

Kaushik also worked in engagements advising clients on performance management, organisation restructuring and learning & development.

Kaushik was promoted as a Senior Consultant and continued to focuse on large scale technology enabled transformation. Kaushik was in Chicago for a year long global JDE implementation and managed a virtually dispersed team team (across US and India). He led the offshore team of eleven consultants  and worked with the onsite change manager, client functional experts across US and Europe, and client’s change director. His other key engagement was in Boston, USA for medical devices major helping implement change for a new financial system.

Kaushik joined Human Capital service line of Deloitte Consulting US as a senior instructional designer. During this tenure he worked on long term technology transformation projects and worked as an integral part of the people, change and learning teams for priority clients. He worked for some key SAP enabled business transformation projects for Levi Straus in San Francisco and from offshore in Hyderabad, India for Zimmer, Burger King and Coca Cola. Kaushik worked on multiple internal initiatives and won the Knowledge Sharing Award - a Deloitte Global recognition.

During his stint in ITC Infotech, Kaushik worked as part of ITC's new greenfield account of Danske Bank. He was part of Danske Bank's elearning team for nearly six months till he moved to Deloitte Consulting. Kaushik was in Copenhagen initially, working closely with the client to help set up the rules of engagement. While onsite he was also designing and developing courses for the Danske Bank's learning management portal. He was one of early members of this new account for ITC Infotech and was instrumental in building a trusted relationship with his client team.

Kaushik worked as a Lead Consultant in the Interactive Media group of ITC Infotech. As an instructional designer, Kaushik was consulting clients, during the design and developing learning content including web based and classroom learning. He also consulted the senior leadership in conceptualising digital media strategies for high value internal communications. Kaushik was also instrumental in assisting the group manager in devising marketing strategies and promoting the services of the Interactive Media group internally and externally.

Kaushik was part of the corporate communication team that reported directly to the CEO. He was involved in all facets of corporate communication. He was responsible for conceiving and developing the production of all offline/online marketing collateral for the various services and products. Kaushik was also managing the content on the corporate website. Additionally, the communications team was also required to provide ad-hoc assistance to do usability reviews of various projects.

He was also responsible for the content analysis, storyboarding and anchoring the production of the interactive media content. During his stint here, Kaushik also worked as a web developer in the digital media integration and managing all aspects of web development.

about:
Patrick Green (Allen) is a Manager in the Deloitte Consulting, Human Capital Practice. As an experienced organization change and transformation leader, he has partnered with clients across numerous industries on projects including M&A integrations, organizational design, operational model development, post-merger integration, system modernization, ERP implementation, and digital/cloud transformation initiatives.

experience.description:
Worked in an agile environment at the E-commerce division of J. Crew, collaborating with product teams, front-end developers and 3rd party firms, and successfully implementing business critical projects
•	Managed an off-shore team to redesign and redevelop the product details p age on the J. Crew website; Successfully migrated the code to Madewell (J. Crew’s sister brand) and J. Crew factory brand
•	Led the implementation of “Product Ratings and Reviews” for J. Crew and Madewell; Collaborated with 3rd party firm (“BazaarVoice”) to use their APIs for reading and loading reviews and ratings
•	Worked with front-end team and product owner to revamp the “gift-guide” page for customers

Worked on trading applications for multiple security classes, including Munis, money market securities and corporate bonds
•	Developed a robust test framework for Muni risk calculator that provided real time risk assessment of Munis
•	Enhanced a trading application to include trading of money market securities, Yankee CDs and CP and corporate bonds 
•	Supported a hedge setup application, which supported hedging strategy for Munis

I build systems to maintain Map Content and Points of Interest data. In my current project I am developing an ETL software to create a data warehouse that can be used for advanced analytics. The technologies I use are Core Java, Spring, SQL, Log4j and Unix. And the environment I work in consists of Oracle 10g (database), Eclipse (IDE), SVN (version control and code repository) and MAVEN (build tool).

Additionally, I have knowledge of Hadoop distributed file systems and  MapReduce framework. I will be using these to implement the next version of Map product database.

My time at Infosys was spent on four major projects over 3+ years. 

1) Mobile Applications for BlackBerry Storm

As a part of Mobile Applications team, I developed various applications for the BlackBerry Storm device. I designed and built ‘TrackMate’ which tracks the path taken by user and amount to be paid while traveling from one point to another. This involved using Google maps and internal GPS of device to track and display the user's real time path.

2) Web based Order Management and Reporting applications for AT&T

I worked on enhancing and maintaining AT&T's web based application that provided its external business partners to access specific operations. I led the detailed analysis of the change request and communicated the complex business logic in simple flow diagrams. I coded in Java and C++, performed rigorous testing and deployed the code on UNIX server boxes. I was awarded the prestigious Quarterly Award for outstanding performance on this project.

3) Web based document submission application for AT&T

I worked on a web based application that allows AT&T's employees to submit documents required to file for an IP application and to check the status of it. I developed new CFML pages  and inserted SQL statements to interact with the backend Oracle database. I also got an opportunity to mentor junior team members on numerous engineering skills, including technical and process oriented standards.

4) Web Access Ordering (WAO) for AT&T's online ordering system

As a part of post-merger integration work, my team was responsible for installing WAO in the US south eastern states. Specifically I worked to enhance WAO application’s pre validation tools, which ensure the correctness of the data submitted. I developed Struts action classes, Form beans and DAOs, and implemented user interface using HTML, JSP, and CSS. I also used multithreading to ensure that data was returned from web service within stipulated time.
