featured.title: Electric Vehicles - Charging Ahead!
featured.subtitle: Saad Qasim, PMP® on LinkedIn

slides.title: Electric Vehicles - Charging Ahead!
slides.subtitle: Saad Qasim, PMP® on LinkedIn
slides.description: The UK and France have recently said they will phase out sales of new petrol and diesel cars by 2040. China, the world’s biggest car market, is mulling a similar move, which would have a significant impact on oil demand. The Indian government has announced that it wants to sell only electric cars within the next 13 years. At long last, it seems that government of Pakistan has woken up to the urgency of promoting this increasingly important technology. First, a National Electric Vehicles Policy was approved in November 2019. It laid out targets that envisioned 30% of all passenger vehicles and heavy-duty trucks sales would be EVs by 2040. In 2020, the government had announced a policy in which only 1% sales tax would be charged for locally manufactured EVs up to 50kWh and light commercial vehicles up to 150 kWh. No Federal Excise Duty will be charged on EVs. In July 2021, the new Auto Policy 2021-2026 contains some important provisions for EVs. Customs Duty on import of certain parts for EVs for local manufacturers will be charged at 1%, while the customer duty on Completely Built up Units will be charged at 10%. There will be no Registration Fees and Annual Renewal Fee for EVs in Islamabad. In this article I will look at some of the challenges EVs will face in Pakistan, and how to overcome them. This will be followed by recommendations for planning a phase-out of old combustion-engine models and replacing them with electric cars. Electric Car adoption in contemporary developing countries like Pakistan Electric cars will help to alleviate the severe air and noise pollution in our cities and towns. Annually, thousands of Pakistanis die or get ill from pollution caused by automobiles. The healthcare costs of such illnesses, productivity lost, and social impacts of lives lost due to pollution are significant. Lead causes brain damage and other particulates cause lung disease, while carbon dioxide adds to global warming. Pakistan is already at severe risk of climate change, hence the need to decrease our transportation emissions urgently. Energy supply In order to prepare the energy infrastructure for the expected rise electricity demand, the planning ministry and various stakeholders will need to forecast the demand and then decide the timelines for rolling out of charging infrastructure across various cities. Assuming that initially EVs will be limited to the big cities, and that the additional load due to charging will be at night, the plan may call for limited additional generating capacity. Baseload plants, such as the coal powered plants already in operation, will be increased in order to meet the new baseloads levels, while no additional peaker plants will be required. Cost - a significant barrier When it comes to buying a new car, the average Pakistani buyer is price sensitive and looks for the best value for money. Budget friendly cars usually offer basic features, thus any successful electric cars would need to cater for modest budgets. Initially, the government will need to offer rebates and subsidies to the buyers of electric cars. This can be funded by imposing a carbon tax on conventional petrol and diesel engine cars. In either case, the end result will be a shift in buying patterns towards electric cars. Early adopters can be encouraged to purchase such cars by getting preferential parking, tax benefits, and so on. While electric cars come in a range of price points, the most popular electric cars in Pakistan will be those that can compete with the incumbent market leaders. Just as the recent influx of imported second-hand Japanese cars proved that they can carve out a niche in the local market, electric car importers and manufacturers will have to do the same. If companies importing EVs are allowed zero duties on new EVs, the cars will quickly become competitive with locally assembled cars. The big incumbent market leaders will have an advantage when it comes to dealer relationships, local manufacturer supply chains and maintenance. They will find it easier to introduce new electric models, but only if their strategy is tailored for electric cars. If they are resistant to change and do not evolve with the changing times, they may well find themselves struggling to face the new players claiming market share. Another incentive for EV adopters will be special Time of Use rates from electric utilities, which encourage use of electricity at certain times (such as late night). Opposition from entrenched market players (Petroleum companies) We can expect the current entrenched interests such as Oil marketing companies (OMCs) and CNG stations to strongly oppose the new market entrants, since it will impact their sales. As the number of EVs slowly increases, the owners of petrol pumps and CNG stations will notice a fall in their customer traffic. As people start charging their EVs at home and at designated public charging points, we may witness the number of petrol pumps shrink. This may be further accelerated by increased EV adoption in the face of rising oil prices. Interoperability for charging - make it mandatory Remember the era of cell phones before the micro USB charger became the standard for charging phones? It was a nightmare for phone users to charge their phones if they didn't have the exact charger available that fitted their phones. The current crop of electric cars have similar charger issues. From Tesla's extra fast supercharger to the Nissan Leaf's average speed charger, each car model charges differently, even if they use the same electric supply. In countries like the US, the issue is being addressed by consortiums of manufacturers with input from the government. In Pakistan, we can learn from the mistakes of other early adopting nations by addressing this issue from the start. The best case scenario would mean all EVs sold here work with every available charging station, and have the latest Level 4 charging capability, meaning they can be charged very quickly, which would address one of the biggest problems owners have; range anxiety. Level 4 charging means you can get about 400 kilometers of charge in just 20 min of charging. Of course, with the high price tag for this kind of capability, its far more likely that the majority of cars will only offer Level 2 or 3 charging. A 50 kW Level 3 charger gets you 80% of a 400 km range in 60 minutes. Mandating charging connector shapes and the charging technology will make life easier for owners in the long run. All cars sold in Pakistan will have to comply with the same connector. Who wants to wait 2 hours for their car to charge enough before continuing your trip to the beach? Range anxiety Range anxiety refers to the problem that most EVs cannot hold enough electric charge for a distance of more than 160 km. Unless you go for a Tesla, which is much more expensive. What's more, you'll need at least half an hour connected to a high-voltage power supply to get any significant charge back into the battery. However, if you're used to charging the battery of your smartphone overnight, it's a similar habit to get into when running an EV. For most city commutes in Pakistan, a fully charged EV should have enough range for the day. And in case you run low, you should be able to pull into a charging station with publicly accessible charging points. Charging Infrastructure That brings us to charging infrastructure. Recently, a major Oil Marketing Company in Pakistan unveiled their EV charging station at a fuel station in Karachi, which features 50kW Rapid chargers. For comparison, in UK the same OMC also offers 150 kW ultra-rapid charging, where 3 types of connectors are available: CHAdeMO, Type 2, and CCS. Tesla offers 250 KW at its newer stations and Porsche demonstrated a 350 KW charger. This is the first such public charging station in Pakistan where an OMC has collaborated with the local utility company to provide charging to EVs. This seems to indicate that local private sector players are preparing for widespread adoption of EVs, although initially at a slow pace. Local Manufacture Encouraging local manufacture of EV components, including the drivetrain, chassis and battery would do wonders for the automobile industry as well as allied sectors. To start with, lithium-ion batteries would need to be imported and then used for assembly, but it would be great if we can utilize the huge lithium reserves in neighboring Afghanistan to set up a giant battery making factory like the Tesla Gigafactory. Smart Metering The nature of EVs makes them well suited for collecting usage statistics and digital measurements. Each EV has onboard sensors and sophisticated software that optimizes vehicle efficiency. The energy they consume while charging can also be metered and used by utilities and the government for planning purposes. Since companies will have to reconfigure their assembly lines for each new EV model introduced here, stricter safety and vehicle compliance measures can be implemented. As a bonus, the road infrastructure upgrade and charging infrastructure to facilitate EV users may present civic bodies an opportunity to uplift each city's hard infrastructure like streets, pavements and traffic infrastructure. Recycling Worn-Out Batteries Once the battery in an EV reaches the end of its life, it will need to be recycled. Currently there aren't enough depleted lithium-ion batteries in early adopter countries to justify large scale recycling plants, but eventually they will need to implement this. Considering the abysmal track record we have of pollution and ignoring safe disposal of hazardous waste in this part of the world, recycling will become all the more important. Batteries contain heavy metals like cobalt and nickel, as well as toxic chemicals which can contaminate groundwater and the soil, if not disposed of safely. The government will have to mandate that sellers of the automobiles will take back defective and worn out batteries for recycling. The requisite technology will either need to be imported and a battery recycling plant set up, or the batteries will need to be shipped to other countries for recycling. Based on how the used batteries are viewed, they could be a treasure for recycling companies, becoming a source for valuable metals like copper and lithium that can be reused by local manufacturers for other products. Public transport and heavy vehicles Many cities around the world are moving towards zero emission vehicles for public transport. Some have chosen hydrogen-powered buses which only emit water, while others are planning to have EV buses or hybrids. With time, the cost of such buses will come down enough for the private and public buses to be electric. Since buses cannot wait long between routes, swapping batteries is a viable solution. Considering the great reception of ridesharing apps in Pakistan, the government can encourage companies like Uber and Careem to invest in EVs and provide incentives such as lower taxes on rides in EVs.

slides.title: Climate Change Mitigation for a Power Utility: Some Project Management Learnings (Part 2)
slides.subtitle: Saad Qasim, PMP® on LinkedIn
slides.description: The first part of this article can be read here. Project Execution Initial Survey Within the stream of Feeder Pillar Box (FPB) raising, the initial scope of work included replacing and raising the foundation of over 500 FPBs, but the scope was later reduced to 338. While the company uses a Geographical Information System (GIS), the locations and mapping of the FPBs were not maintained in the system. The project team for FPBs consulted the GIS subject matter experts, resulting in a new survey of the target sites, and a list of all the target FPBs, along with their GPS coordinates, photos, specifications, and their current condition. The GIS already contained details of all the Ring Main Units (RMUs), but a survey was still carried out to determine the specifications and current condition of each RMU, as well as to verify the data captured in the GIS. Vendor onboarding and Coordination Once the vendors were selected, they underwent mandatory HSE training and were onboarded. The documentation requirements, reporting standards, and communication plan was communicated to all the vendors. Unfortunately, the vendors did not comply with the reporting standards, and documentation was often delayed. Coordination was patchy, with a large lag in the material consumption reporting, progress reporting, and QA issues. These issues remained throughout the project but slightly improved with time. Workarounds for these communication gaps had to be found. Lesson Learnt: Constant communication is essential, with the escalation of communication issues when necessary. Multiple channels for communication can be provided, but all parties need to commit to using them. While the mapping of the FPBs was a huge help, unfortunately, several FPBs had been tagged wrongly during the survey, and there were multiple duplications in the IDs. Data inconsistencies continued to be a problem in reporting and complicated the reconciliation of the work completed by the field team. Due to the new nature of work, the pace initially was slower than planned. In line with project management principles, greater risks and issues were encountered towards the start, which lessened as the project progressed. Permitting and External Approvals Getting permission for excavation, road cutting, and other civil work in public spaces required coordination and paperwork to be submitted, along with payments to be made as per the Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs). The lack of cooperation and slow response from government agencies was an impediment that led to delays. The project team used contacts within the company who were familiar with the agencies and could expedite permitting, but during the actual execution, permits and SOPs were less helpful than using personal relations and people skills to get the work done. This was a valuable lesson for future projects of a similar nature. Lesson Learnt: Using PR and the power of informal networking can help influence external stakeholders with major influence on your project, as opposed to formal communication. Roadblocks and Obstacles Internal Approval for Shutdown Getting approvals for shutdown required prior notice and coordination with the Operations team, which was operating under multiple constraints. Due to the fluid nature of Operations work, shutdowns were sometimes canceled or delayed, leading to the planned work getting delayed. During the holy month of Ramadan, the company was forced to decrease the pace of work due to a ban on shutdowns. Because this risk was anticipated early, it was decided that work would continue on civil work on the FPB stream, which didn’t require shutdowns. Lesson Learnt: Such interventions or other delays would have been easier to plan and forecast if critical paths had been defined by using a PMIS. Material shortages Like other countries around the world, Pakistan was also impacted by Covid-19 and the attendant supply chain disruptions. Some critical material was unable to be delivered in time, so the Project Manager had to arrange it from another department through negotiation skills, and support from the Project Sponsor. The risk was successfully mitigated, resulting in only a slight delay. Change Management Overcoming resistance from consumers was a challenge, particularly as the field execution necessitated shutdowns for over 12 hours at a time. The project team sent out notices to inform the customers beforehand, while also engaging with difficult customers personally to allay their concerns. The Marketing team sent some affected customers cookies as a gesture for the inconvenience faced. Some customers were also concerned about the appearance of the raised FPBs and their placement near their houses. Such issues had to be tackled tactfully and addressed through negotiation and collaboration. Quality Management For a project of this size, the quality criteria to be checked during inspections need to be shared with the execution team well before execution, including a form for inspection plus a system to capture images, etc. This allows the execution team to pay particular attention to avoid those issues. Avoidance of issues is much less costly compared to rectification. Lesson Learnt: Formulate and share the checklist for QC well in advance with the execution team and include possible points of failure. Quality requires transparency and well-organized information, that is repeatable and easily verifiable. In this project, spot checks, sampling, and QC were done by multiple parties, whose methodology and game plan weren’t transparent. In line with the hybrid approach, the technical specifications, and checklist of work to be done were shared early by the project team to the vendors. The first batch of FPB and RMUs were treated as a pilot, allowing the team to study possible issues, then tweak the approach for later FPBs to avoid a repeat of quality issues. Lesson Learnt: Alignment with QC for periodic ‘sprints’ could have greatly increased the impact of this approach. Closure Closure activities for the project involved scope validation by multiple teams. However, planning for closure was not formally captured in any plan, and aligning the teams for carrying out inspections required coordination that wasn’t planned out in detail earlier. Vendors submitted invoices through courier according to their Scope of Work in their Contracts, and after validation of delivery, invoices were closed. Automation and the use of workflows would have greatly streamlined this process. On the other hand, by this stage of the project, the bulk of the fieldwork was completed, but due to faulty survey data, there were some inconsistencies in the invoices that had to be corrected. Lesson Learnt: The major lesson learned here is that frequent data quality checks, data management, and simple sanity checks like checking for duplicate data using Excel etc. can go a long way. To conclude, this project is the first of many that will be needed to mitigate or offset the impact of climate change in Karachi. Ensuring that the proper methodology is followed and the knowledge gained from previous projects is applied in the future will certainly help deliver better value for both utilities and their customers.

slides.title: Climate Change Mitigation for a Power Utility: Some Project Management Learnings (Part 1)
slides.subtitle: Saad Qasim, PMP® on LinkedIn
slides.description: Introduction From extreme temperatures, extreme weather events of increased frequency and intensity, to rising sea levels threatening coastal areas, climate change is directly impacting communities, resulting in billions of dollars’ worth of damage. Karachi is no stranger to extreme weather events. In 2015, severe heatwave resulted in the loss of hundreds of lives. In 2020, rainfall during the annual monsoon broke 90-year records, resulting in the inundation of most of the city. The standing water and lack of drainage resulted in multiple deaths through electrocution and drowning, and power was cut off in several localities to prevent further loss of life and minimize equipment damage. The flooding was so bad, that power wasn’t restored to some areas for over 10 days. The sole power utility that provides power to Karachi had to undertake measures to address this new threat of urban flooding. As a member of the project team, I obtained some insights into the planning and execution for this project, and in this article I share some lessons learnt. Project Initiation The project to make the network more resilient to flooding and extreme weather events was initiated due to external pressure, including several court cases in the Pakistan legal system, as well as strong demands from the government to avoid a repeat of the 2020 situation. As such, the responsibility for the initial feasibility and business case was given to the Planning department. In order to determine the scope of the project, the project team first performed analysis on outage data obtained from the Network Management System, then prioritized those feeders that had the longest and most severe outages. Feeders are the highest level in the network hierarchy for electricity distribution. Next, target feeders were shortlisted based on business criticality, which resulted in 45 feeders being included in the scope. Options for engineering solutions were explored, including raising critical infrastructure off the ground so that it remains dry during urban flooding. However, the root cause of the aforementioned flooding was not addressed as that lies under the purview of other stakeholders, such as civic agencies and the government. During the project, these stakeholders were also engaged and they agreed to fix the drainage issues to prevent flooding. The overall budget for the short term and medium-term infrastructure upgrades was estimated, using figures from subject matter experts. Approval for the project was sought from the Board of Directors, keeping in mind the urgency and business need for minimizing power disruption. The project had a time constraint, as the major work needed to be completed before the 2021 annual monsoon, which typically starts in July. Project Planning Once the project was approved, the project team was finalized, and the planning work began. Keeping in mind the complexity and cross-functional nature of the project, team members were included from Planning and Engineering, Procurement, HR, Quality, HSE, Distribution, External Affairs, Finance, Marketing, and Civil Works. The scope was divided into streams, such as raising of Ring Main Units (RMUs), raising of Substations, etc. and each stream was assigned a Project Manager. Overall project oversight was assigned to the Management Committee, while day to day responsibility lay with the Head of Planning and Engineering. Project Methodology The project methodology, while not formally discussed, evolved over time to a hybrid model, a combination of waterfall and Agile. Waterfall is the traditional method of project management, where the project proceeds in sequence from Initiation, to Planning, Requirement Gathering, Execution and then Closure. Agile is a more recent methodology, which features an adaptive and iterative approach to projects, focusing on delivering value to the customer as quickly as possible. The planning phase mostly followed the waterfall methodology, while the execution was blend of Agile and waterfall. From my experience of working within the streams of Ring Main Unit Raising and Feeder Pillarbox Raising, the hybrid model offered some advantages and disadvantages that will be discussed later. Planning Process The planning process continued for 4 months, September to December, while execution started in late December. The planning process needed to be thorough and extensive for multiple reasons. First, the engineering nature of the project meant that new technical drawings and technical specifications had to be made and network redesign needed to be conducted. Secondly, the scope of work had to be progressively elaborated, new resources had to be hired, a list of materials to be procured for each stream prepared, location surveys done and high-level project plans made. Pre-Execution Surveys To collect information about the scope of work, field teams carried out survey of the areas that had experienced flooding and power disruption. Teams identified and tagged company assets such as Substations, RMUs and FPBs to be upgraded. However, this was all done manually rather than through a customized online system. If carried out in a more structured manner, duplication of effort could have been avoided later. This survey did not include taking GPS coordinates and photos. Management Plans While there were no individual plans for Scope Management, Schedule Management, Cost Management, Resource Management, Procurement Management, Stakeholder Management, Quality Management, Communication Management and Risk Management, all of these were discussed and documented at one point or another in the project planning. If these plans had been individually created and followed, a lot of ambiguity and risk would have been avoided. Due to the lack of a company wide Project Management Office (PMO), the Organizational Process Assets that can formalize and ease the planning and documentation of such plans were not available in many cases. The downside of this lack of formal plans for a few knowledge areas led to some sub-optimal outcomes, including unforeseen risks, coordination issues with other departments, a lack of a document management system to capture knowledge and track learnings. The lack of a PMIS (Project Management Information System) such as MS Project, Primavera etc. also made it much harder for the team members in charge of project tracking, scheduling and resource management to carry out their work. There was no Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) or WBS dictionary, so scope wasn’t well documented. These tools help define what needs to be done, the acceptance criteria for each task, and what resources will be required for it. On the other hand, detailed checklists for services provided and materials consumed were created and provided to the vendors for easier material managements and cost management. On the plus side, thanks to strong support from the Project Sponsor and buy-in from other departments, the project was able to overcome resistance from multiple stakeholders and achieve quicker outcomes than usual. Not getting bogged down in documentation also allowed the project teams for each stream to be more agile, adapting to changing circumstances and uncertainty with speed. Procurement Once the scope became clear, Requests for Proposals (RFPs) were floated by the Procurement team. The vendors were invited to visit the sites to understand the technical and environmental challenges. A cross-functional team performed a technical evaluation of the proposals based on organizational guidelines, then shortlisted the best proposals. Finally, Procurement did a commercial evaluation and selected the vendors. In parallel, Procurement was tasked with expediting the delivery of the required materials in bulk, as many of the materials are routinely used by the utility, but the expected consumption was much higher than normal. The existing SAP Material Management and SharePoint based procurement solution was proposed for team members to requisition materials, and issue materials from the stores located across the city. The system would also help in cost reconciliation and budget control. For the sake of brevity, the story of this project and the lessons learnt will continue in the next post.

slides.title: Software Challenges in Smart Grid Projects
slides.subtitle: Saad Qasim, PMP® on LinkedIn
slides.description: This article builds on the previous introduction to Smart Grid Implementation that I wrote here. Once you have selected the vendor, based on proposed design, project experience, features offered, financials, and other criteria, the next step is to finalize the scope of your smart grid implementation. Every Smart Grid project has some common features, while at the same time each project has some requirements that are unique to the company or project. The optimum value of a Smart Grid system can only be unlocked if the data is accurate, timely and relevant. If any of these three conditions are not met, the efficacy of the system is greatly reduced. The Smart Grid consists of three parts, the smart devices or sensors that will measure energy consumption or related data such as voltage, the Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) that allows the meters to communicate with the utility via a telecommunications network, and the software that collects, processes and displays the data from the meters. The software is usually the challenging part of the implementation, which may come as a surprise to many. The actual installation and deployment of the hardware is fairly straightforward and once the Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) are in place, the deployment becomes routine for the organization. Ideally, the communications network in the coverage area has the capacity and infrastructure in place to handle the project requirements. Otherwise, the telecommunications partner for the AMI data transmission may require additional investment to expand the capacity and coverage. A utility that previously was operating with conventional meters will not find it difficult to switch over to AMRs or Smart Meters when it comes to installation and regular maintenance. This is because the process for storing, transporting, inspecting and installing the meters is mostly in line with existing (conventional meter) practices. The main differences lie in preparing the meters for installation and commissioning, since there is some programming and setup involved for each device. The real challenge lies in organizing the vast amounts of data related to meters, consumers, network hierarchy and geographical mapping. The optimum value of a Smart Grid system can only be unlocked if the data is accurate, timely and relevant. If any of these three conditions are not met, the efficacy of the system is greatly reduced. From the consumer billing perspective, smart meters are helpful to remotely collect usage data accurately, regularly and without human intervention. Smart meters can be used during normal operations to easily adjust consumer electricity pricing from peak to off-peak demand hours. And during an outage, they can let repair crews know instantaneously where service is down on a building-by-building level. The personnel and transport costs associated with meter reading can be saved by this system. These savings have to be weighed against the additional capital and operating costs of the AMI and associated systems. In order for the billing to take place, the meter needs to communicate with the head-end, the system that receives the data stream from each smart meter and makes it available for other systems. In order to ensure that the head-end is able to communicate effectively with the billing system, a middleware is needed to act as a buffer. This middleware can vary from project to project based on the specific tools and software used. This is known as an MDM or Meter Data Management system. The MDM acts as a liaison between the head-end and the Billing Management System (BMS). It also becomes the repository for the usage data and events generated by the smart meters. Without the MDM, the BMS will not have the usage data in a form that it can process and use for billing. Unlike a conventional meter, which is read monthly or bimonthly, smart meters can send readings every minute or even more frequently, depending on requirements. This poses the problem of converting the consumption into a form that the BMS can accept. A common way to do this is to designate a periodic billing date for each meter, which is treated as a monthly billing date. The total energy consumed by the customer during this period is calculated and then communicated to the MDM, which passes on the info to the BMS. This calculation can be fairly simple, such as summing up all of the energy consumed over the time period, or more complex, if taking into account Time of Use (TOU) parameters, Reactive Power and Active Power. Once the BMS knows exactly how many KWhs have been consumed, as well as the total off-peak and on-peak pricing details associated with that customer, the bill is generated.

publications.description: The heightened regulatory scrutiny and enforcement of the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) and other country-specific anti-corruption statutes are increasingly rendering global automotive manufacturers vulnerable to significant compliance and reputation risks. Although the generic risks of doing business in emerging and growth markets are fairly well understood, the challenge many companies face is understanding the specific risks of a country and the local business operations and confirming that the internal controls and business processes in place are sufficient to address them.  This article provides a perspective for reducing risk and improving global compliance and transparency through the application of anti-corruption-specific internal controls.

As General Manager for Deloitte’s BenefitsIQ benefits administration solution, I am passionate about transforming benefits administration for public sector organizations. BenefitsIQ harnesses the power of AI to help federal, state, and local government organizations modernize and future-proof their benefits programs—delivering greater efficiency, accuracy, and security. Our platform not only helps organizations reduce administrative complexity and minimize risk of fraud, waste, and abuse, but it also empowers employees to make smarter benefit choices.

With over 30 years of consulting experience, I have led large-scale technology and business transformation initiatives across the healthcare, insurance, and public sectors. My career spans leadership roles including Americas Delivery Leader—where I grew Deloitte’s delivery capabilities across the US, Mexico, and LATAM—and US Offering Leader for Core Industry Solutions, driving industry-centric technology innovation for clients nationwide.

Previously, as National Leader for Deloitte’s Healthcare Information Technology practice, I guided organizations through complex systems integration, operational redesign, and digital transformation projects. My expertise covers the full spectrum of benefits and insurance administration, from clinical information systems and revenue cycle improvements for providers, to group and individual insurance solutions for payers.

I am committed to helping government and public sector organizations leverage technology to deliver better outcomes for their employees and constituents. Whether leading mission-critical IT implementations, optimizing operational processes, or advising on emerging technologies, I bring a strategic, results-driven approach to every engagement.

Specialties:
•	Benefits administration transformation for government and public sector
•	Large-scale technology and business transformation
•	Healthcare and insurance systems integration
•	Project leadership and operational redesign
•	AI-enabled solutions for public sector challenges

Let’s connect to discuss how technology can drive better benefits outcomes for your organization.

education.schoolName: University of Illinois Chicago School of Law
education.degree: Master of Laws (LLM) and Juris Doctor (JD)
education.description:
Besides learning how to work under pressure, the most important tool one learns in law school is that there is no way to know everything, but by asking the right questions and having the right knowledge about how to find out the answers, you can figure just about anything out.

Oh the world of Intellectual Property is beautiful.  IP is the intersection of business, creativity, invention, and the law.  IP consists of trademarks, patents, copyrights, trade secrets, and rights of publicity (among others).  I love IP, it allows me to utilize the knowledge for my own enterprises, and to share the knowledge with clients, friends, and family alike.  Thanks to John Marshall Law School, and the impeccable staff and leaders there, I was trained and guided by the best.  Looking forward to being a life-long student of IP.
education.insights: Activities and societies: President of the Justinian Society of Lawyers, JMLS 2011

education.description: CIDE Study Abroad Program through the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign.  The City of Bilbao is a gem, my home away from home.  I miss the rainy mornings, and green mountains, being a 45 minutes ride from San Sebastian, and spending nights near the famous Guggenheim Museum.  I'll be back one day, hopefully as a property owner and small business builder.

The University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign is an epic educational and social institution.  You most likely will not be the smartest person in any classroom, and the work/ play balance is perfect for the determined and serious academic, but adventurous socialite.  I miss the walks on the Quad (when it's summer), being surrounded by students and scholars, and learning about ancient history.  One thing you get out of being a Classical Civ Major is that you realize history is written by people.  People have biases.  Your job is to piece all the sources together to form your own puzzled truth of the historical past.  Advocate for your interpretation of the facts.  Consider the reverse argument, prove why it is not true.  This lesson would later serve me well in law school.

One of my favorite lessons: "AUDACES FORTUNA IUVAT" - "Fortune favors the bold/ brave."  This is my personal mantra.  In my own words, good fortune follows those who are brave enough to believe in their dreams.

headline: Managing editor-Production, Deloitte Insights Publishing
about: Experienced managing editor with a demonstrated history as a versatile, self-motivated team player. With 30 years in the publishing industry, I’ve worn more hats than I can count in environments ranging from global enterprises to start-ups. I’ve spent the last 10 years as part of two groups of world-class researchers within Deloitte, first with Bersin and then transitioning to Deloitte Insights, the firm's flagship destination for thought leadership. I'm most energized by roles that mix long-term planning and project management with hands-on, detail-oriented work.

experience.description:
Deloitte Insights is the signature thought leadership platform for research generated throughout the various Deloitte ecosystems, producing daily leading-edge content on the web as well as a bi-annual print magazine, Deloitte Insights Magazine. My accomplishments and responsibilities at Deloitte Insights have included:

- Design, implementation, and management of newly launched production team. As the first manager of this brand-new function, I am responsible for the production of 400-600 publications annually. This includes a balance of hands-on project management, oversight of projects managed by my team members, and support of publications produced by teams in EMEA and APAC. Implementation of the new production function has been critical to successful management of a vastly increased workload.

- Design, implementation, and management of newly launched project management platform (Workfront). Included researching and interviewing potential providers; conducting needs discovery with team leads; creating budget, project plans/schedules, and team training in collaboration with technical project team; managing evolution of data from and sunsetting of previous system; and ongoing platform management. 

- Management of the publication calendar. Responsible for scheduling all content, requiring daily management of shifting priorities and competing stakeholders. 

- Management of quality control. Responsible for quality control for all publications. Created or overhauled all QC processes. 

- Management of 11 direct reports, all as part of a fully remote global team. This includes hiring, management, and development of both editorial production and assistant editor staff in the United States, India, and EMEA.

- Built collaborative relationships across multiple global research teams, enabling me to manage complex team dynamics and build trust in the Deloitte Insights brand across the Research and Insights function.

Deloitte’s Bersin™ team provides proprietary human capital research to more than 5,000 member organizations. My accomplishments and responsibilities at Bersin included:

- Successfully launched a new and expanded position as managing editor. This role combined a greatly widened scope of departmental responsibilities with an increased workload of individual editorial projects, all while maintaining or exceeding production and quality expectations. 

- Day-to-day management of editorial production of 100+ publications annually for a 40+-person global team. Evaluated and developed manuscripts; assigned work to editorial team (both in-house and freelance); managed production schedules and publishing cadence; tracked team responsibilities and deliverables. Also responsible for a wide variety of tasks supporting day-to-day team functioning, including maintaining our project management platform; leading editorial/design team “scrum” meetings; leading monthly research planning meetings with a variety of team leads; and creating and maintaining editorial reference materials and process documentation.

- Maintained individual editorial role. Reviewed and provided direction for work in progress; edited to improve overall content, cohesion, tone, organization, readability, and audience segmentation.

- Volunteered to co-lead department implementation of a new cloud-based project management platform (Wrike) and created a prototype for a new publications report using that platform. Coordinated with our large team to create and confirm scheduling and assignments for our editorial “roadmap” (400+ projects), becoming an early adopter, super-user, and trainer for this platform. Created a report designed to pull data from that project management platform, synthesizing hundreds of schedules into a highly visual and easily digestible format distributed throughout Deloitte Human Capital Consulting as a critical tool for cross-functional planning with marketing, sales, etc.

In 2006, I began my own contract editorial business providing copy editing, developmental editing, project management, proofreading, and photo research to trade and academic publishers as well as independent authors. I have worked with clients including McGraw-Hill Professional, Triumph Books, McKinsey & Co., the Wisconsin Historical Society Press, Red Line Editorial, Crowe Horwath, the Milbank Memorial Fund, and Hillcrest Media Group.

Responsible for all editorial production for a small publisher focusing on sports, entertainment, and gift books. Management of entire book production process, including tracking and directing all production work flow and creating and managing schedules. Hired, trained, and managed in-house associate editor and editorial assistant. Managed freelance writers, copyeditors, fact checkers, proofreaders, indexers, and designers; interacted with authors, agents, photo houses, packagers, and other contributors. Created and/or restructured all editorial production processes, including creation of a 30-page house editorial style document and checklists for each stage; revision and/or creation of editorial filing and archiving systems.
Managed the production of multiple trade and educational titles each season.

headline: Contracts Manager at Deloitte
about:
As a Virginia-licensed attorney specializing in Corporate and Contract Law, I combine years of experience in government, commercial, and real estate contracting to deliver strategic legal solutions. I excel in contract analysis, drafting, negotiation, and risk mitigation—helping clients navigate complex agreements while protecting their interests and unlocking new opportunities.

My approach focuses on clear communication, proactive legal guidance, and meticulous attention to detail. Whether advising on high-stakes deals or routine agreements, I am dedicated to ensuring every contract is compliant, resilient, and aligned with my clients’ objectives.

experience.description:
Contract lifecycle management: Oversee all phases of the contract process—from initial proposal through execution, amendment, renewal, and closeout—ensuring timely and accurate contract administration.

Support proposal development: Collaborate with pursuit and proposal teams to review RFPs and contribute to contract sections of bids or new business opportunities.

Draft, review, and negotiate contracts: Prepare and revise a wide range of agreements, including service agreements, NDAs, subcontractor agreements, and statements of work, ensuring compliance with Deloitte standards and client requirements.

Risk Management: Analyze contract terms to spot potential legal, operational, and financial risks and propose mitigation strategies, working closely with Legal, Risk, and senior leaders.

Advisory: Provide guidance to engagement leaders, managers, and stakeholders regarding contract terms, obligations, and implications, enabling informed decision-making.

Third-Party Negotiation: Engage with client legal/procurement teams and third-party suppliers to resolve contractual issues and finalize mutually beneficial agreements.

Ensure regulatory compliance: Rigorously monitor contract terms to confirm adherence to all applicable government laws, rules, and policies (e.g., FAR, DFARS, GSA schedules), and coordinate compliance.

Ensure contractual compliance: Advise project leaders and delivery teams on nuanced government contract obligations, such as reporting, invoicing, records retention, small business participation, and flow-down clauses.
